title: After Finishing My Study Abroad at Tulane University in the United States
paragraphs: I had never studied abroad before, and since I had always lived at my parents' home, I wanted to try living alone abroad once, so I applied for study abroad. In addition, the United States is the most advanced country in medicine, and it had the appeal that I could talk with doctors and patients in the English I had been practicing, so I decided to study in the United States and was allowed to study at Tulane University in the United States for two months. Tulane University is in New Orleans, a town in the southern United States, and is a core hospital of the American South. Seventy percent of New Orleans' population is Black, and I think most of the patients were Black. Although it is in America, it is a town influenced by France, and the food is quite delicious. Crawfish, which we do not eat in Japan, is also part of the food culture. It is also the birthplace of jazz, jazz is played everywhere around the town, and in April the Jazz Festival is held lively, and I was able to enjoy concerts by famous bands. On the other hand, it is a town with poor public safety that is often hit by hurricanes.

[About the clerkship] I rotated through obstetrics and gynecology for two weeks and orthopedic surgery for four weeks. In obstetrics and gynecology, I did one week of clerkship at the clinic of University Medical Center and one week of perinatal clerkship at Lakeside Hospital. At the clinic they did checkups of pregnant women in early pregnancy and gynecological examinations and tests. There were many third-year Tulane students, and every day I went to the patients with the residents and those students, doing ultrasound, history taking and pelvic examinations. On Friday afternoons I took lectures by obstetrics and gynecology doctors with the local students. Meeting American patients and getting to know many local students was a good experience. The second week's clerkship at Lakeside Hospital started at 5 AM, so I got up at 3:30 AM at the earliest. There was no bus to Lakeside Hospital, so I went by car with a local student. There, pregnant women close to delivery and postpartum women were hospitalized, and I observed deliveries and was allowed into cesarean sections. Childbirth in the United States is almost all painless delivery, so unlike in Japan the pregnant women did not scream, and births took place in a quiet atmosphere. I was allowed into cesarean sections several times. At the first cesarean section, from a large pregnant woman first came a giant baby of over 4 kilograms, and then a normal baby of about 3 kilograms came out, so it turned out she was carrying large twins, and I was greatly surprised, thinking, so this is American size. The mornings were early, but being present at the birth of a life made me very happy, and I could not help thinking that babies are cute in both Japan and America. Being able to rotate through obstetrics and gynecology in the United States and notice the differences from Japan, and also the appeal that is no different from Japan, was a great gain.

For the remaining four weeks I rotated through orthopedic surgery. Tulane's orthopedic surgery is divided into the Trauma unit, Reconstruction unit, Rheumatoid unit, Sports unit and Pediatric unit, and I was allowed to rotate through the four except Pediatric, one week each. In the Trauma unit the main work was operations on trauma patients, and I think most were ankle fractures. Next, in the Reconstruction unit I was allowed into total hip arthroplasty and total knee arthroplasty. These operations were very impressive, and I never got tired of them however many times I was in. In Japan I had not been much in the surgical field, so seeing a hip joint like the one I had hurt myself was very fresh. In the next, Rheumatoid, there was not much going on, so I was allowed into reconstruction operations. In the final week, the Sports unit, I was in hamstring decompression surgery and total shoulder arthroplasty. They were operations rarely seen in Japan, so they were fresh. Besides the clerkship, I also had fun, such as being taken to a beer garden by an orthopedic resident.

[Summary] During the preparation period for study abroad I broke my leg and had to be hospitalized, and it was uncertain whether I could go, but I managed to make it in time and go. Both in preparing for and during my study abroad I was supported by so many people. Dr. 西尾, Dr. 長谷川 and Dr. 粕谷, who negotiated with Tulane University many times and listened to my concerns. The orthopedic and rehabilitation doctors who operated on me and discussed the plan afterward. My parents, who paid for the hospitalization and the study abroad funds. All my Nagoya University clerkship friends who helped me at various times at my destination. Thank you very much. Thanks to all of you, I think I was able to have a very valuable experience that will lead to my future. I am truly glad I was able to go study abroad. I would like to make use of my experience of being injured and hospitalized, and of talking with wonderful doctors in the United States and being allowed to take part in operations, in my work as a doctor, which will probably begin next year. If I have the chance, I would like to go study in the United States or other countries again.
